```{r}
source("_common.R")
source("_figures.R")
library(patchwork)
```

In a **randomised trial** the investigator assigns the intervention by chance.
Randomisation makes the arms comparable in everything, measured or not, so a
difference in outcomes is caused by the intervention or by chance, and the
confidence interval accounts for chance. There is no confounding to adjust for
at baseline. What remains can still bias a trial: who leaves it, who does not
take the treatment, and how the outcome is measured. This page covers the trial
designs, then two designs that are not trials but look like them (before-after,
method comparison), and diagnostic accuracy studies.

## Parallel randomised trial

::: {#fig-rct}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.8
boxes <- data.frame(id = c("el", "ra", "a", "b", "fa", "fb", "an"), x = c(0, 2.6, 5.2, 5.2, 7.8, 7.8, 10.4), y = c(0, 0, 0.8, -0.8, 0.8, -0.8, 0),
                    label = c("Eligible,\nconsenting", "Randomised", "Intervention", "Control", "Follow-up,\noutcome", "Follow-up,\noutcome", "Compare as\nrandomised (ITT)"),
                    role = c("other", "confounder", "exposure", "other", "other", "other", "outcome"))
links <- data.frame(from = c("el", "ra", "ra", "a", "b", "fa", "fb"), to = c("ra", "a", "b", "fa", "fb", "an", "an"))
both(flow_fig, boxes, links, w = 2.1, h = 0.95)
```
A parallel trial. The comparison that keeps the protection of randomisation is by assigned arm: intention to treat (ITT).
:::

**Estimates.** The effect of being *assigned* the intervention, as risk
difference, risk ratio, NNT, odds ratio, hazard ratio or mean difference.

**Strengths.** Randomisation removes confounding, known and unknown; blinding
removes bias in measuring the outcome and in co-interventions; the strongest
evidence for an effect.

**Limitations.** Expensive; selected participants and strict protocols (results
may not apply to every patient); short follow-up; impossible or unethical for
harmful exposures. **Non-adherence** dilutes the intention-to-treat effect, and
the alternatives are no longer randomised comparisons: *as treated* (by the
treatment received) and *per protocol* (only those who followed it) are
confounded by whatever made people stop [@hernan2017]. Losses to follow-up
related to prognosis bias any analysis.

**Analysis.** Binary outcome: risks per arm, RD with NNT, RR (*Frequencies ▸
Independent Samples*), or logistic regression. Continuous: difference in means
(t-test), or **ANCOVA** adjusted for the baseline value, which is more precise.
Time to event: Kaplan-Meier and Cox. Adjusting for strong prognostic factors
increases precision. For odds and hazard ratios it also changes the estimand,
from marginal to conditional ([Measures and models](guide-measures.qmd)).

**Interpretation.** "Risk of pancreatitis 17% with placebo and 9% with
indomethacin: 8 fewer cases per 100 patients treated, NNT 12." The odds ratio of
the crude comparison is the effect on the population of patients, not on an
individual with given characteristics.

```{r}
trial_table("indomethacin_ercp", "pancreatitis")
```

**In studysim.** *Rectal indomethacin to prevent post-ERCP pancreatitis*, randomised trial; *Biases* ▸
*Non-adherence* adds as-treated and per-protocol rows to the key.

## Cluster randomised trial

::: {#fig-cluster}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
cl_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    set.seed(4)
    cl <- data.frame(cluster = 1:12, cx = rep(1:6, 2) * 2.2, cy = rep(c(2.2, 0), each = 6), arm = sample(rep(c("intervention", "control"), 6)))
    ppl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:12, function(k) { a <- runif(14, 0, 2 * pi); r <- sqrt(runif(14)) * 0.75
        data.frame(cluster = k, x = cl$cx[k] + r * cos(a), y = cl$cy[k] + r * sin(a), arm = cl$arm[k]) }))
    ggplot() + ggforce_circle(cl, p) +
        geom_point(data = ppl, aes(x, y, colour = arm), size = 1.6) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = c(intervention = p$role[["exposure"]], control = p$role[["other"]]), name = NULL) +
        coord_equal() + theme_fig(mode) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
ggforce_circle <- function(cl, p) {
    t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 60)
    circ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cl)), function(k) data.frame(cluster = k, x = cl$cx[k] + 0.95 * cos(t), y = cl$cy[k] + 0.95 * sin(t))))
    geom_polygon(data = circ, aes(x, y, group = cluster), fill = NA, colour = p$muted, linewidth = 0.5)
}
both(cl_fig)
```
Twelve clusters (villages, schools, practices) randomised as a whole. People in a cluster resemble each other, so the trial has less information than its number of people suggests.
:::

**What it is.** Groups are randomised: villages, schools, wards. Necessary when
the intervention acts on groups (hand-washing campaigns, a new ward protocol)
or when individuals would contaminate each other.

**Strengths.** Feasible for community interventions; avoids contamination.

**Limitations.** Outcomes of people in the same cluster are correlated (the
**intraclass correlation**, ICC), so the effective sample size is smaller: the
design effect is 1 + (m − 1) × ICC for clusters of m people. Few clusters means
chance imbalance between arms.

**Analysis.** A mixed (multilevel) model with a random intercept per cluster
(**GAMLj**), or cluster-robust standard errors. Ignoring the clusters gives
confidence intervals that are too narrow.

**Interpretation.** A mixed logistic model gives an odds ratio *within* clusters
(conditional); a model with robust errors gives the population-average one, which
is closer to 1.

**In studysim.** *Handwashing and childhood pneumonia* (counts of pneumonia), *Vitamin A and child mortality*, cluster randomised trial; vary the intraclass correlation.

## 2×2 factorial trial

Two interventions randomised independently, so each participant gets one of
four combinations. One trial answers two questions, *if the interventions do not
interact*: each main effect is estimated by comparing everyone with and without
it. With an interaction the main effects are averages over the other
intervention, and the trial needs to be powered to detect the interaction.
Analyse with both treatments in the model (*ANOVA*, logistic or Cox regression)
and test their product term. In studysim: *Aspirin and beta-carotene in male physicians* (aspirin and
beta-carotene).

## Crossover trial

::: {#fig-crossover}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 2.4
co_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    d <- data.frame(seq = rep(c("sequence AB", "sequence BA"), each = 3), xmin = rep(c(0, 4, 5.2), 2), xmax = rep(c(4, 5.2, 9.2), 2),
                    what = c("A", "washout", "B", "B", "washout", "A"))
    ggplot(d) + geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 3 - as.numeric(factor(seq)) - 0.35, ymax = 3 - as.numeric(factor(seq)) + 0.35, fill = what), colour = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
        geom_text(aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = 3 - as.numeric(factor(seq)), label = what), colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
        annotate("text", x = c(2, 7.2), y = 2.65, label = c("period 1", "period 2"), colour = p$fg) +
        scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = p$role[["exposure"]], B = p$role[["mediator"]], washout = p$role[["other"]]), guide = "none") +
        scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:2, labels = c("sequence BA", "sequence AB")) + labs(x = "time", y = NULL) +
        theme_plot(mode) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
}
both(co_fig)
```
A 2×2 crossover: each participant receives both treatments, in a random order, separated by a washout.
:::

**What it is.** Each participant receives both treatments in random order, for
stable chronic conditions and treatments whose effect wears off.

**Strengths.** Each participant is their own control: with outcomes that are
correlated within a person, far fewer participants are needed.

**Limitations.** Only for reversible effects and stable conditions; a
**carryover** effect of the first treatment into the second period biases the
comparison; dropouts lose both periods.

**Analysis.** Paired t-test of the outcome under A and under B (one row per
person: *Repeated measures: wide*), or a mixed model with treatment and period
as fixed effects and the participant as cluster (long layout), which also
estimates the period effect.

**In studysim.** *Antihypertensive drug* or *Bioequivalence of two formulations*, 2×2 crossover;
*Design options* ▸ period and carryover effects.

## Longitudinal trial

::: {#fig-longitudinal}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
sc_lead <- load_scenario(lib, "lead_succimer")
lg <- simulate_study(sc_lead, "blood_lead", "longitudinal", 60, sc_lead$order, seed = 2, options = list(dropout = 0.25), key = FALSE)$data_raw
lg_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    m <- aggregate(blood_lead ~ visit + treatment, lg, mean)
    ggplot(lg, aes(visit, blood_lead, colour = treatment)) + geom_line(aes(group = id), alpha = 0.25) +
        geom_line(data = m, linewidth = 1.5) + geom_point(data = m, size = 2.5) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = c(placebo = p$role[["other"]], succimer = p$role[["exposure"]]), name = NULL) +
        labs(x = "visit (0 = baseline)", y = "blood lead (ug/dL)") + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(lg_fig)
```
Sixty children of a simulated longitudinal trial (*Succimer for lead-exposed children*), with 25% dropout: thin lines are children (some stop early), thick lines the mean of those still seen at each visit.
:::

Repeated visits give the trajectory of the effect, but participants drop out,
and dropout usually depends on how they were doing. Comparing only the
completers at the last visit is biased when dropout depends on earlier values. A
**linear mixed model** with all visits (random intercept per participant,
treatment by visit) is valid when dropout depends on values already observed
(missing at random). jamovi: **GAMLj** *Mixed Models*; repeated-measures ANOVA
uses completers only.

## Before-after study (no control group)

::: {#fig-rtm}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
set.seed(9)
true <- rnorm(800, 8, 1)
rtm <- data.frame(before = true + rnorm(800, 0, 0.7), after = true + rnorm(800, 0, 0.7))
cut <- quantile(rtm$before, 0.7)
rtm$enrolled <- rtm$before > cut
rtm_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    e <- rtm[rtm$enrolled, ]
    ggplot(rtm, aes(before, after)) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = p$muted, linetype = "dashed") +
        geom_point(aes(colour = enrolled), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.6) + geom_vline(xintercept = cut, colour = p$role[["confounder"]]) +
        annotate("point", x = mean(e$before), y = mean(e$after), size = 5, shape = 21, fill = p$role[["outcome"]], colour = p$fg, stroke = 1) +
        annotate("label", x = mean(e$before) - 0.3, y = mean(e$after) + 1.6, hjust = 1, colour = p$fg, size = 3.6,
                 fill = if (mode == "dark") "#1f2226" else "#ffffff", label.size = 0,
                 label = sprintf("enrolled: mean %.2f before, %.2f after", mean(e$before), mean(e$after))) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = p$role[["other"]], `TRUE` = p$role[["exposure"]]), guide = "none") +
        labs(x = "value before", y = "value after (no treatment)") + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(rtm_fig)
```
Regression to the mean. Nobody is treated, but people enrolled because their first value was high (above the vertical line) have lower values when measured again: part of a high value was chance, and chance does not repeat.
:::

Everyone is measured before and after the intervention. The mean change mixes
the effect with the natural course of the condition, with what else happened
meanwhile and, when people are enrolled *because* their values were high, with
**regression to the mean** [@barnett2005]. A paired t-test tests the change,
not the effect. A control group (a trial) is the remedy; failing that, enrol on
a separate baseline measurement or repeat it. In studysim: *Metformin vs placebo on HbA1c*,
before-after, with *Enrol only above percentile*.

## Diagnostic accuracy study

::: {#fig-diagnostic}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
auc <- 0.82; delta <- sqrt(2) * qnorm(auc); cutp <- delta / 2
dg_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    x <- seq(-3.5, 3.5 + delta, length.out = 400)
    d <- rbind(data.frame(x = x, dens = dnorm(x), group = "without the disease"),
               data.frame(x = x, dens = dnorm(x, delta), group = "with the disease"))
    cols <- c(`without the disease` = p$role[["other"]], `with the disease` = p$role[["outcome"]])
    a <- ggplot(d, aes(x, dens, colour = group)) +
        geom_area(data = d[d$group == "with the disease" & d$x > cutp, ], aes(fill = group), alpha = 0.3, colour = NA) +
        geom_area(data = d[d$group == "without the disease" & d$x > cutp, ], aes(fill = group), alpha = 0.3, colour = NA) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_vline(xintercept = cutp, colour = p$fg, linetype = "dashed") +
        annotate("text", x = cutp + 0.1, y = 0.42, label = "cut-off", hjust = 0, colour = p$fg, size = 3.6) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) + scale_fill_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
        labs(x = "marker", y = NULL) + theme_plot(mode) + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
    th <- seq(-4, 4 + delta, length.out = 300)
    roc <- data.frame(fpr = 1 - pnorm(th), tpr = 1 - pnorm(th, delta))
    b <- ggplot(roc, aes(fpr, tpr)) + geom_abline(colour = p$faint, linetype = "dashed") + geom_line(colour = p$role[["exposure"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
        annotate("point", x = 1 - pnorm(cutp), y = 1 - pnorm(cutp, delta), size = 3.5, colour = p$fg) +
        annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = 0.25, label = sprintf("AUC %.2f", auc), colour = p$fg, size = 4) +
        coord_equal() + labs(x = "1 - specificity", y = "sensitivity") + theme_plot(mode)
    a + b + plot_layout(widths = c(2, 1))
}
both(dg_fig)
```
A marker that is higher in people with the disease. At a cut-off (dashed), the shaded area of the diseased is the sensitivity and that of the non-diseased one minus the specificity; moving the cut-off traces the ROC curve.
:::

**What it is.** A sample of people *in whom the test would be used*, all
receiving the index test and the reference standard (the best available way of
knowing who has the disease).

**Estimates.** Sensitivity and specificity at a cut-off, the ROC curve and its
area (AUC), likelihood ratios, and the predictive values (PPV, NPV), which also
depend on the prevalence.

**Biases.** **Spectrum bias**: studying severe cases and healthy volunteers
instead of the patients where the test is needed overstates accuracy
[@ransohoff1978]. **Partial verification**: when only test-positives (and some
negatives) get the reference standard, sensitivity is overstated and
specificity understated. An imperfect reference standard, and a cut-off chosen
on the same data, flatter the test.

**Analysis.** 2×2 table at a cut-off; ROC analysis (**meddecide**, **psychoPDA**);
logistic regression to combine markers, validated on other data.

**In studysim.** *PSA and prostate cancer*, *High-sensitivity troponin for myocardial infarction*, diagnostic design; *Biases* ▸ spectrum and verification.

## Method comparison

Two methods measure the same quantity in the same people (a new device against
the standard). A correlation coefficient says nothing about agreement: two
methods can correlate perfectly and differ by 10 units. The **Bland-Altman**
analysis plots the difference against the mean of the two and reports the mean
difference (bias) and the **limits of agreement**, mean ± 1.96 SD of the
differences, within which 95% of the differences fall [@bland1986]. Whether
those limits are acceptable is a clinical decision. A slope in the plot shows a
proportional bias.

::: {#fig-ba}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
sc_nh <- load_scenario(lib, "nhanes_blood_pressure")
mc <- simulate_study(sc_nh, "sbp", "method_comparison", 300, character(), seed = 4, key = FALSE)$data_raw
mc$mean <- (mc$sbp_a + mc$sbp_b) / 2; mc$diff <- mc$sbp_b - mc$sbp_a
ba_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    m <- mean(mc$diff); s <- sd(mc$diff)
    ggplot(mc, aes(mean, diff)) + geom_point(colour = p$role[["exposure"]], alpha = 0.6, size = 1.4) +
        geom_hline(yintercept = m, colour = p$fg) + geom_hline(yintercept = m + c(-1.96, 1.96) * s, colour = p$role[["outcome"]], linetype = "dashed") +
        geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = p$role[["confounder"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
        annotate("text", x = max(mc$mean), y = m + c(-1.96, 0, 1.96) * s + 1.5, hjust = 1, colour = p$fg, size = 3.4,
                 label = c("lower limit of agreement", sprintf("mean difference %.1f", m), "upper limit of agreement")) +
        labs(x = "mean of the two methods (mmHg)", y = "B - A (mmHg)") + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(ba_fig)
```
Bland-Altman plot of two simulated blood pressure devices (*Blood pressure in US adults*, method comparison): method B reads `r round(-mean(mc$diff), 1)` mmHg lower on average, and the sloping line shows that the gap grows with the pressure (proportional bias).
:::

## What to remember

| design | estimand | main threat | analysis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parallel trial | effect of assignment (ITT) | non-adherence, loss to follow-up | as randomised; ANCOVA, Cox |
| Cluster trial | effect of assigning the cluster | correlation within clusters | mixed model or robust errors |
| Factorial | two main effects | interaction | both treatments and their product |
| Crossover | within-person effect | carryover | paired t-test or mixed model with period |
| Longitudinal | effect over time | informative dropout | linear mixed model |
| Before-after | change, not effect | regression to the mean, secular trend | add a control group |
| Diagnostic | sensitivity, specificity, AUC | spectrum, partial verification | patients like those who will be tested |
| Method comparison | agreement | proportional bias | Bland-Altman, not correlation |
